lessons.title: Turn field notes into a structured technical report draft with Claude or ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Convert raw site or field notes into an organized first-draft technical report structure, ready for your review, calculations, and sign-off.
lessons.goal: Produce a structured first-draft technical or field report from raw notes, with every observation traceable to what you actually recorded.
lessons.whyItMatters: Field reports and inspection write-ups are constant in engineering practice, and turning scrawled notes into a clean, structured document is a slow, repetitive task. AI can organize your raw observations into a professional report structure fast, freeing time for the parts of the job that need engineering judgment. But it never visited the site, never took a measurement, and cannot verify a condition, a code reference, or a safety implication - every recommendation, calculation, and conclusion in the final report has to come from you.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Your raw field notes as taken - bullet points, abbreviations, and rough measurements are fine. Do not rewrite them into prose first; the AI works best from your actual notes.
steps: Gather your raw field/site notes exactly as recorded, including any measurements, photo references, or abbreviations.
State the report type, project name/number, site visit date, and your role (e.g. structural inspection, punch list, condition assessment).
Paste the raw notes into the prompt below rather than pre-editing them into full sentences.
Ask for a fixed report structure: purpose and scope, observations by location or system, conditions noted, and an open placeholder for recommendations.
Instruct the model to use only the notes provided and to flag anything ambiguous rather than guessing at what you meant.
Read the draft against your original notes and photos, correcting any paraphrase that shifts the meaning of an observation.

Add your own engineering recommendations, calculations, and conclusions yourself - these are never generated by the AI - then route the report through your firm's standard review and stamping process.
lessons.prompt:
You are helping me convert raw field notes into a structured first-draft technical report. This is a non-final draft for my own review - not a finished or approved engineering report, and it contains no independent engineering judgment, calculations, or conclusions of your own.

Rules:
- Use ONLY the notes provided below. Do not add observations, measurements, conditions, or conclusions that are not explicitly in the notes.
- Do not offer opinions on severity, code compliance, structural adequacy, or safety - leave a bracketed placeholder like [ENGINEER TO ASSESS] wherever a professional judgment is needed.
- If a note is abbreviated or unclear, write '[CLARIFY: unclear note - confirm meaning]' rather than guessing what it means.
- Preserve specific numbers, measurements, and locations exactly as given - do not round, estimate, or generalize them.

Draft a report with this structure:
1. Project / site information (from notes)
2. Purpose and scope of visit
3. Observations, organized by location or system
4. Conditions noted (factual only, no severity ratings)
5. Recommendations - leave as [ENGINEER TO COMPLETE]

Field notes:
[PASTE RAW FIELD NOTES]
lessons.explanation: Organizing observations by location or system instead of dumping them chronologically is what makes a report usable to someone who wasn't on site, and it's a natural task for AI once you give it your raw notes verbatim. The [ENGINEER TO ASSESS] and [CLARIFY] placeholders are the real safeguard: they stop the model from quietly supplying a severity judgment, a code opinion, or a guess at what an abbreviated note meant, and instead put a visible flag exactly where your professional judgment has to go. Preserving numbers exactly as given matters because a model that 'cleans up' a measurement - rounding 3/8 in to a fraction that reads cleaner - can silently introduce an error that matters structurally.
lessons.example:
Field notes: 'NW corner, 2nd flr slab - hairline crack ~14ft run, max width 1/16in. Rebar exposed at col C4 base, approx 6in section, corrosion visible. Roof drain #3 - ponding, standing water 1/2in noted at 2pm, dry weather.'

Draft output excerpt: 'Observations - Second Floor, Northwest Corner: Hairline crack observed in slab, approximately 14 ft in length, maximum width 1/16 in. Column C4, Base: Exposed reinforcing steel over approximately 6 in section; corrosion visible. [CLARIFY: extent/depth of corrosion not specified in notes.] Roof, Drain #3: Ponding observed, standing water approximately 1/2 in deep at time of observation (2:00 PM), dry weather conditions. Recommendations: [ENGINEER TO COMPLETE].' Every figure matches the note exactly, and the one place where judgment would be needed - assessing the corrosion - is flagged instead of assumed.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, take real or practice field notes from a recent site visit and generate a draft using this prompt. Compare every observation in the draft against your original notes and photos before adding your own recommendations.
lessons.expectedResult: A structured draft report where every observation, measurement, and location traces directly back to your field notes, with clarification flags on anything ambiguous and an open placeholder for your own professional recommendations.
commonMistakes: Letting the model infer a severity or code-compliance opinion from a factual observation instead of leaving that placeholder for your own assessment.
Accepting a rounded or 'cleaned up' measurement instead of checking it exactly matches what you recorded in the field.
Skipping the review against original notes and photos because the draft reads fluently and looks complete.
Treating a report generated this way as final without it going through your firm's standard engineer review and stamping process.
lessons.proTip: Keep a standard notes shorthand you use consistently in the field (e.g. always noting location, then observation, then measurement in that order) - the more consistent your raw notes, the more reliable the structured draft, and the less clarification flagging you'll need to resolve.

lessons.title: Explain a technical concept to non-technical stakeholders with Claude or ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn a technical decision, constraint, or trade-off into a plain-language explanation a client, owner, or board member can actually follow - without losing the substance.
lessons.goal: Produce a plain-language explanation of a technical concept or decision for a non-technical audience that keeps the real substance intact.
lessons.whyItMatters: Engineers constantly have to explain why a design choice was made, what a constraint means for cost or schedule, or why a change is necessary - to clients, owners, boards, or the public. A poorly explained technical decision can stall approvals and erode trust even when the underlying engineering is sound. AI is genuinely useful for reframing jargon into plain language quickly, but you're the only one who can confirm the simplified version hasn't quietly dropped or distorted something that matters.
steps: Write down the technical concept or decision in your own accurate, technical terms first - don't start from a vague description.
State who the audience is and what they actually need to walk away understanding (a decision to approve, a cost implication, a risk).
Ask for the explanation in plain language, with a short glossary of any term you can't avoid using.
Instruct the model not to soften or omit any safety, cost, or schedule implication in the process of simplifying.
Ask for an analogy only if it doesn't misrepresent how the underlying engineering actually works.
Review the plain-language version against your original technical description and correct anything that changed meaning, not just wording.
Use the explanation as a speaking or writing aid - you remain responsible for what you actually tell the stakeholder.
lessons.prompt:
You are helping me translate a technical engineering concept into plain language for a non-technical audience. Accuracy matters more than simplicity - do not omit or soften any safety, cost, or schedule implication in order to make the explanation shorter or easier to follow.

Technical concept (in my own words): [DESCRIBE THE CONCEPT/DECISION ACCURATELY]
Audience: [e.g. city council, homeowner client, non-technical project sponsor]
What they need to understand or decide: [STATE THE PRACTICAL STAKES]

Rules:
- Do not introduce a technical claim, number, or implication that isn't in my description above.
- If an analogy would help, only use one that doesn't misrepresent how the underlying engineering actually works - flag it as an analogy, not a literal description.
- Include a short glossary (2-4 terms) for any unavoidable technical term.
- End with one sentence stating clearly what decision or action the audience is being asked to understand or approve.

Write the explanation in plain language, 150-250 words.
lessons.explanation: Starting from your own accurate technical description - rather than asking the model to explain the concept from scratch - keeps the simplification process bounded: it can only reword and reframe what you gave it, not fill gaps with generic engineering knowledge that may not apply to your specific case. Banning omission of safety, cost, or schedule implications matters because the most common failure in 'plain language' technical writing is quietly dropping the caveat that made the original explanation complicated in the first place. The closing decision sentence keeps the explanation useful in practice - stakeholders need to know what they're actually being asked to understand or approve, not just get an easier version of the theory.
lessons.example:
Technical concept supplied: 'We're specifying a deeper foundation than the client expected because geotechnical testing found a soft clay layer at 6ft depth that won't support the standard footing design without excessive settlement over time.' Audience: homeowner client. What they need to understand: why the foundation cost is higher than the original estimate.

Output: 'When we tested the soil under your home site, we found a layer of soft clay a few feet down. A standard foundation resting on that layer would slowly sink unevenly over years, which can crack walls and floors. To avoid that, we need to build the foundation deeper, past the soft layer, onto more stable soil - similar to why a table with one short leg needs a shim to stay level, except here we're changing the foundation itself so it never needs one. This adds cost now but avoids a much more expensive repair later. Glossary: Settlement = the ground and foundation sinking over time. Geotechnical testing = testing the soil to see what it can safely support. What you're being asked to approve: the deeper foundation design and its added cost.' Nothing about the risk or the reason for the added cost was softened.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, take a real technical decision from a current project and run it through this prompt for a specific stakeholder audience. Read it back against your original technical description and confirm nothing material was lost.
lessons.expectedResult: A plain-language explanation that a non-technical stakeholder can follow, that preserves every safety, cost, and schedule implication from your original technical description, ending with a clear statement of what they're being asked to understand or decide.
commonMistakes: Letting a simplifying analogy misrepresent how the engineering actually works, which can mislead a stakeholder into an inaccurate mental model.
Allowing cost or safety caveats to get dropped in the simplification because they made the explanation less clean.
Skipping your own technical description and asking the model to explain the concept generically, which risks it filling gaps with assumptions that don't match your actual project.
Presenting the explanation as if it were the final word rather than checking it against your own understanding before speaking or sending it.
lessons.proTip: Keep a short personal glossary of the analogies that have worked well with clients or boards in the past (e.g. how you explain settlement, load paths, or drainage), and paste them in as reference examples - it keeps your explanations consistent across projects instead of reinventing the framing each time.

lessons.title: Build a reusable review checklist for documents and drawings with Claude
lessons.summary: Generate a structured, discipline-specific checklist for reviewing specs, drawings, or submittals, so first-pass reviews are systematic instead of relying on memory.
lessons.goal: Produce a reusable, editable review checklist for a specific document or drawing-set type that an engineer applies with their own judgment, not an automated pass/fail tool.
lessons.whyItMatters: Reviewing drawing sets, specifications, and submittals under deadline pressure is exactly where a systematic checklist earns its keep - it's how experienced reviewers avoid missing a recurring issue. AI drafts a strong starting checklist for a familiar document type fast, but it does not know your current adopted code edition, your firm's standard of care, or the specific project context - every item still needs your own verification against the actual documents and current code.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A clear sense of the discipline, document/drawing type, and code edition you're building the checklist for. If your firm has an existing QA/QC checklist, have it ready to paste in so the AI builds on your standards rather than generic ones.
steps: State the discipline (structural, civil, MEP, etc.), document or drawing-set type, and the current adopted code/standard edition.
If your firm has an existing QA/QC checklist, paste it in and ask the model to build on it, not replace it.
Ask for a checklist organized by category (e.g. general/coordination, loads and design criteria, details, code compliance) rather than one flat list.
Instruct the model to mark any item where a specific code section, load value, or current requirement matters with a verification flag, since it cannot confirm the currently adopted edition.
Review the checklist and remove or adjust anything that doesn't match your firm's actual practice or the project's governing code.
Test the checklist against a real drawing set or submittal and note anything you caught that the checklist prompted but would otherwise have skimmed past.
Save the refined checklist as a firm resource, dated and version-tagged, and mark it a review aid, not authoritative code guidance.
lessons.prompt:
You are helping draft a first-pass review checklist for engineering documents or drawings. This is a review aid for a licensed engineer, NOT a substitute for code research, calculations, or professional judgment.

Rules:
- Organize the checklist by category, not as one flat list.
- For any item where a specific code section, load value, dimensional requirement, or current edition matters, add the tag [VERIFY CURRENT CODE/STANDARD] rather than stating a specific numeric requirement as fact.
- Phrase every item as a question to check ('Are gravity loads shown consistent with the design criteria stated on the general notes sheet?'), never as an assertion of what the answer should be.
- If I provide an existing firm QA/QC checklist below, build on and refine it rather than replacing it with generic content.

Build a review checklist for:
Discipline: [e.g. structural]
Document/drawing type: [e.g. steel connection design submittal]
Governing code/standard and edition: [STATE EDITION]
Existing firm checklist (if any): [PASTE OR WRITE 'NONE']

Format: category headers, each with 3-6 checklist questions.
lessons.explanation: Phrasing every item as a question rather than an assertion keeps the checklist from silently injecting a code requirement or design conclusion into what should be a neutral review aid - the reviewer still has to look at the actual drawing and confirm the answer. The [VERIFY CURRENT CODE/STANDARD] tag does the real safety work here: code editions, load values, and referenced standards change and vary by jurisdiction, and the model cannot know which edition governs your specific project, so it flags exactly where the checklist's usefulness ends and your own code research begins. Anchoring to an existing firm QA/QC checklist, when available, keeps the output aligned with your actual standard of care instead of generic industry boilerplate.
lessons.example:
Request: checklist for reviewing a steel connection design submittal, structural discipline, governing code AISC 360 and the locally adopted IBC edition, no existing firm checklist supplied.

Output checklist (excerpt): 'General / Coordination: Do connection design loads match the reactions shown on the structural framing drawings? Are member sizes referenced in the connection calc consistent with the drawing set? Design Criteria: [VERIFY CURRENT CODE/STANDARD] Does the stated design basis reference the correct current edition of AISC 360 and the applicable IBC edition? Details: Are bolt grade, size, and quantity clearly called out and consistent between the calc and the detail? Is weld size and type shown on the detail consistent with the calc? Code Compliance: [VERIFY CURRENT CODE/STANDARD] Does the connection meet the minimum eccentricity and edge distance requirements of the governing standard?' Each item is a question to check against the actual submittal, not a stated numeric answer.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, build a checklist for a document or drawing type you regularly review. Apply it to a real submittal and note at least one issue the checklist prompted you to check that you might otherwise have skimmed past.
lessons.expectedResult: A categorized, question-based checklist tailored to your discipline and document type, with code-sensitive items clearly flagged for independent verification, that measurably speeds up a real review without replacing your judgment or calculations.
commonMistakes: Treating the checklist as an authoritative code reference instead of a memory aid that still requires your own current-code and calculation verification.
Skipping the [VERIFY CURRENT CODE/STANDARD] items instead of actually confirming them against the governing code edition before relying on the checklist.
Reusing a checklist across a materially different structure type or jurisdiction without regenerating or adjusting it.
Letting the checklist replace your firm's actual QA/QC process instead of building on and refining it.
lessons.proTip: Keep a version-controlled master checklist per document type and, after each real review, ask the model 'Based on what I found in this review that wasn't on the checklist, what should be added?' - this grows the checklist from real practice instead of staying static.

lessons.title: Research codes, standards, and precedents with citations using Gemini Deep Research
lessons.summary: Use Gemini Deep Research's cited web research to quickly survey applicable standards, guidance documents, and comparable precedents for a design question - as a starting point you verify against the actual current source.
lessons.goal: Produce a source-cited research summary of applicable codes, standards, and precedents for a specific engineering question, with every claim independently verified against the current official source before use.
lessons.whyItMatters: Engineers regularly need to survey what standard applies, how a similar condition has been handled elsewhere, or what guidance exists for an unusual design situation - and doing that research manually across scattered PDFs and databases is slow. Gemini Deep Research browses many sources over several minutes and returns cited answers, making it easy to see where a claim comes from and follow the link, which is a real advantage over an ungrounded chat response. But a citation link is not proof the code section is current, correctly quoted, or the right adopted edition for your jurisdiction - that verification is the engineer's responsibility, every time, before anything is designed or stamped based on it.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A specific, well-scoped research question - not 'what codes apply to my project' generally, but a defined question like 'what does ASCE 7 require for X' or 'how is Y condition typically detailed.' A Gemini account; Deep Research is free on the Flash tier, and Google AI Pro (about $19.99/mo) raises the quota and uses the stronger Gemini 3.1 Pro model.
steps: Write a specific, narrow research question rather than a broad topic - specificity produces better, more checkable citations.
State your jurisdiction and, if known, the code/standard edition you believe applies.
Open Gemini and start a Deep Research session rather than a normal chat, so it runs genuine multi-step web research across many sources instead of a single-pass answer.
Ask it to answer using cited sources and to distinguish code/standard text from general industry commentary or forum discussion.
Ask it to flag if it cannot find the specific current edition and is relying on an older or unclear version.
Wait for the report - Deep Research browses many sources over several minutes to longer, it isn't instant.
Open every cited source yourself and confirm the quoted text actually appears in it, in the section referenced.
Cross-check the code edition and any amendment history against your jurisdiction's official adopted-code page, not just the cited source.
Keep a research note recording the question, the answer, the sources checked, and the date - standards and adopted editions change.
lessons.prompt:
I need a cited research summary on a specific engineering standards/precedent question. Prioritize official code text, standards-body publications, and government/regulatory sources over forums, blogs, or vendor marketing content. Clearly distinguish code/standard requirements from general commentary or opinion.

Research question: [STATE A SPECIFIC, NARROW QUESTION]
Jurisdiction: [STATE JURISDICTION]
Code/standard and edition I believe applies (if known): [STATE OR WRITE 'UNKNOWN - PLEASE HELP IDENTIFY']

For each source cited:
- Quote or closely paraphrase the specific relevant text
- Note the code/standard edition and publication date
- Flag clearly if you are uncertain whether this is the current adopted edition for my jurisdiction

If you cannot find an authoritative source for part of the question, say so explicitly rather than inferring an answer from general knowledge.
lessons.explanation: Gemini Deep Research's value here is the citation trail, not the summary text itself - after several minutes of multi-step browsing across many sources, the report is only a map telling you which official sources to go open and read yourself. Asking it to separate code/standard requirements from commentary matters because standards questions frequently surface forum discussions and vendor guidance that sound authoritative but aren't the actual requirement. The edition/date flag is the most important line in the output: code editions are adopted on a jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction basis and often lag the standards body's latest publication by years, so a technically correct citation to the newest edition can still be the wrong one for your actual project.
lessons.example: Research question: 'What does ASCE 7 require for wind exposure category determination for a low-rise building in open terrain?' Jurisdiction: a specific US county. Output: a summary citing the relevant ASCE 7 section defining Exposure Categories B, C, and D with the criteria for each, noting the publication edition (e.g. ASCE 7-22) and flagging: 'This jurisdiction's adopted building code may reference an earlier edition of ASCE 7 (e.g. ASCE 7-16 via the 2021 IBC) - confirm the adopted edition with the local building department before use.' The engineer then pulls the actual ASCE 7 section text from the standard itself and confirms with the local building department which edition is currently adopted before using it in a design calculation.
lessons.exercise: In your own Gemini account, research a real code or standards question from a current project as a Deep Research brief. Open at least two cited sources and confirm the quoted text matches, then check the code edition against your jurisdiction's official adopted-code reference.
lessons.expectedResult: A cited research summary where you've personally verified at least one specific quoted requirement against its original official source, and confirmed the code edition against your jurisdiction's actual adopted code before relying on it for design work.
commonMistakes: Using the cited summary directly in a calculation or design decision without opening the actual source and confirming the quote and section number.
Assuming a citation to the newest published edition of a standard is automatically the one your jurisdiction has adopted.
Treating a forum thread or vendor guide that Deep Research surfaces as equivalent authority to the actual code or standard text.
Skipping the jurisdiction-specific amendment check - many jurisdictions adopt a base code with local amendments that override sections of the base standard.
lessons.proTip: For any standard you research often, keep a personal running note of the exact edition and any local amendments your jurisdiction has adopted, and paste that into future Deep Research briefs - or save it as standing instructions in a Gemini Gem - so you're not re-verifying the same edition question every time.

lessons.title: Draft meeting minutes and RFI / change-order communications with Claude or ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn rough meeting notes into clean minutes, and turn a field issue or scope change into a clear, well-documented RFI or change-order communication.
lessons.goal: Produce accurate, well-organized meeting minutes and RFI/change-order drafts built strictly from facts and decisions you supply, ready for your review before distribution.
lessons.whyItMatters: Meeting minutes, RFIs, and change-order documentation are the project record - they get referenced months later in disputes, claims, and schedule reviews, so precision and traceability matter more than polish. AI can turn rough notes into a clean, consistently formatted document fast, but it cannot know what was actually decided, agreed, or observed in the field - every fact has to come from you, and the draft is never distributed until you've confirmed it matches your own record of what happened.
steps: For minutes: gather your raw meeting notes, attendee list, and any action items discussed. For an RFI/change order: gather the specific issue, its location, and the facts driving it.
State the document type (minutes, RFI, or change-order notice) and the project/meeting/issue reference number.
Paste your raw notes or facts, not a pre-written narrative - let the AI do the structuring.

Ask for the standard structure for that document type: minutes need attendees/decisions/action items; an RFI needs the question, drawing/spec reference, and requested response date; a change order needs scope, cost/schedule impact placeholder, and reference documents.
Instruct the model not to characterize fault, cause, or contractual responsibility - state facts and open questions only.
Review the draft against your actual notes, correcting anything paraphrased in a way that changes what was said or decided.
Add any cost, schedule, or contractual language yourself before the document goes out, then distribute through your normal project-record channel.
lessons.prompt:
You are helping me draft a [DOCUMENT TYPE: meeting minutes / RFI / change-order notice] from notes I provide. This is a draft for my review before distribution - not a final project record until I confirm it.

Rules:
- Use ONLY the notes/facts provided below. Do not add attendees, decisions, causes, or facts not stated.
- Do not assign fault, cause, or contractual responsibility - state facts, questions, and open items neutrally.
- Where cost or schedule impact would need to be stated, leave a placeholder like [COST/SCHEDULE IMPACT TO BE DETERMINED] rather than estimating one.
- Preserve specific dates, reference numbers, and drawing/spec citations exactly as given.

For MINUTES, structure as: date/attendees, items discussed, decisions made, action items (owner + due date).
For an RFI, structure as: RFI number/date, question, relevant drawing/spec reference, reason for the question, requested response date.
For a CHANGE ORDER NOTICE, structure as: reference number, description of the change, reason/trigger, affected drawings/specs, cost/schedule impact placeholder.

Notes/facts:
[PASTE RAW NOTES OR ISSUE DETAILS]
lessons.explanation: Locking the output to one of three fixed structures - minutes, RFI, or change-order notice - matches how these documents are actually used and referenced later, so nothing gets buried in loose prose. Banning fault or cause characterization keeps the draft strictly factual, which matters because these documents routinely surface in contractual disputes where an offhand AI-generated phrase about a party's error could be read as the engineer's own conclusion. The cost/schedule placeholder exists because those numbers require your own estimating judgment and contract knowledge - never a plausible-sounding guess from the model.
lessons.example:
Notes supplied for an RFI: 'Detail 5/S-301 shows beam bearing on wall but wall thickness on plan A-102 doesn't match - plan shows 8in, detail assumes 12in wall. Need clarification before fabrication, steel order due in 2 weeks.'

Output: 'RFI #014 - Date: [date]. Question: Please clarify the wall thickness at the beam bearing condition shown in Detail 5/S-301. Reference: Detail 5/S-301 assumes a 12 in wall; Architectural Plan A-102 shows an 8 in wall at the same location. Reason for question: Discrepancy between structural detail and architectural plan must be resolved before steel fabrication. Requested response date: [date, noting steel order deadline in 2 weeks].' No cause or fault is assigned to either drawing - the discrepancy is simply stated as a fact requiring clarification.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, draft either a set of meeting minutes from a real (or practice) meeting or an RFI from a real coordination issue, using this prompt. Check the draft against your actual notes line by line before treating it as ready to send.
lessons.expectedResult: A clean, correctly structured draft - minutes, RFI, or change-order notice - where every fact, date, and reference traces to your original notes, with no fault characterization or invented cost/schedule figures, ready for your final review before distribution.
commonMistakes: Letting the model characterize which party caused an issue, which can create contractual exposure if the document later becomes part of a dispute record.
Accepting a placeholder cost or schedule estimate the model supplied rather than leaving it for your own actual estimate.
Sending the draft out as the official project record without checking it against your actual meeting notes or field observations first.
Losing specific drawing/spec references or dates in the rewrite - always verify these against your notes character for character.
lessons.proTip: Keep your firm's standard RFI and change-order numbering and distribution list as a short reference block you paste into every prompt - it keeps generated drafts consistent with your actual project-record format instead of a generic template.

lessons.title: Build reusable documentation templates for your engineering discipline
lessons.summary: Design a standardized, guardrail-built-in prompt template your team can reuse across recurring documentation tasks - inspection reports, RFIs, calc summaries - instead of everyone improvising from scratch.
lessons.goal: Design a versioned, reusable documentation template for a recurring task type in your discipline that bakes in grounding rules, professional-judgment placeholders, and code-verification reminders by default.
lessons.whyItMatters: As AI use spreads across an engineering team, inconsistent ad hoc prompting produces inconsistent quality and inconsistent safeguards - one engineer's careful placeholder discipline doesn't help if the next person skips it. A shared, versioned template turns the practices from earlier lessons in this path into a team standard, applied automatically instead of re-derived every time someone opens a chat window.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A recurring documentation task your team performs often (e.g. inspection reports, RFI drafting, submittal review checklists) and, ideally, one or two real examples to test the template against.
steps: Pick one recurring, well-defined documentation task your team performs often - not a broad catch-all.
List the fixed guardrails every version of this task must include: grounding-only rules, professional-judgment placeholders, code/standard verification flags, and a non-final label.
Identify the variable parts: what changes each time (project, discipline detail, document type, output structure).
Draft the template with clear bracketed placeholders for the variable parts and fixed language for the guardrails.
Test the template on 2-3 real or realistic inputs and check the guardrails hold across different cases, not just the easy one.
Version the template (e.g. v1.0), documenting what it's for, what it's not for, and any known limitations.
Store it in a shared, firm-approved location and set a review date to revisit it as tools, codes, and practices change.
lessons.prompt:
You are helping me design a reusable prompt template for a recurring engineering documentation task, for use across my team. This is a meta-task: design the template itself, not a one-off document.

Context:
Task type this template is for: [e.g. structural steel connection review checklist]
Who will use it: [e.g. project engineers, EITs]
Output needed each time: [e.g. categorized checklist, structured report draft]
Fixed guardrails that must appear in every use of this template (do not weaken or remove these):
1. Use only the supplied notes/data; no invented observations, measurements, or facts.
2. Insert a bracketed placeholder wherever professional engineering judgment, a calculation, or a code-compliance opinion is needed - never generate one.
3. Flag any item where a current code edition, standard, or jurisdiction-specific requirement matters, rather than stating it as settled fact.
4. Label all output 'DRAFT - engineer review and stamp required as applicable' and state it does not replace calculations or code review.
5. Preserve all numeric values, dates, and references exactly as supplied - never round, estimate, or generalize them.

Design a template with:
- A short reusable rules/guardrails block (incorporating the 5 fixed items above, written naturally)
- Clear bracketed placeholders for the variable parts: [PROJECT/DISCIPLINE DETAIL], [DOCUMENT TYPE], [DESIRED OUTPUT STRUCTURE], [SOURCE NOTES/DATA]
- A one-line usage note for teammates on when this template applies and when it doesn't
lessons.explanation: Separating fixed guardrails from variable placeholders is what makes a template actually reusable and auditable across a team: anyone fills in the brackets, but the safety language - judgment placeholders, code-verification flags, numeric-preservation rules - never gets accidentally dropped because someone is in a hurry. Testing on multiple real inputs before rollout catches cases where a guardrail gets ignored on messier data than the first clean example. Versioning and a review date matter specifically in this field because code editions, standards, and firm QA/QC practices change on a schedule the template needs to keep up with.
lessons.example: Template built for 'geotechnical field observation report,' used by field engineers: a fixed preamble stating the five guardrails in natural language, followed by placeholders '[PROJECT]: ___', '[SITE VISIT DATE]: ___', '[SOURCE FIELD NOTES]: ___', and an output structure request for observations by test location with a recommendations placeholder. A usage note reads: 'v1.0 - for routine field observation write-ups only. Not for final geotechnical reports or bearing-capacity recommendations, which require full engineer analysis.' The team tests it on three past site visits, confirms the [ENGINEER TO ASSESS] placeholder consistently appears wherever a soil condition needed interpretation, and adopts it as the team standard.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, build a template for one recurring documentation task from your own practice, following the structure above. Test it on two different real inputs and note anywhere a guardrail needed strengthening.
lessons.expectedResult: A versioned, documented template with fixed guardrail language and clear variable placeholders, tested against real project data, ready to store as a shared team resource with a defined scope and review date.
commonMistakes: Building a template so broad ('write any engineering document') that the variable parts overwhelm the fixed guardrails and output quality becomes inconsistent again.
Skipping the test phase and rolling the template out to the team without checking guardrails hold on real, messy field data.
Letting the template go unversioned and undocumented, so no one knows which version is current or why a change was made.
Treating the template as a permanent fix instead of scheduling a review date, given how often codes and standards get updated.
lessons.proTip: Keep a short changelog alongside each template version noting what real-world gap or near-miss prompted each guardrail addition - this turns the template into institutional memory for the team, not just a formatting shortcut.

lessons.title: Turn meeting notes into a project proposal and fee letter draft with Claude or ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Convert notes from an initial client meeting into a structured project proposal and fee letter draft, ready for your scope and fee judgment before it goes out.
lessons.goal: Produce a structured first-draft project proposal and fee letter from meeting notes, with scope and fee figures clearly marked for the architect to complete.
lessons.whyItMatters: Turning a productive client meeting into a polished proposal is time-consuming, and delay can cost you the commission to a firm that responds faster. AI can organize your meeting notes into a clean, consistent proposal structure quickly, but it has no basis for setting your actual scope of services, fee structure, or contract terms - those come entirely from your professional judgment and your firm's standard terms, never from a generated guess.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Your raw notes from the client meeting - project description, client goals, budget hints, timeline - and your firm's standard fee structure or a sense of the fee range you intend to propose.
steps: Gather your raw meeting notes: project description, client goals, site info, budget/timeline mentioned.
State the project type and that this is a proposal/fee letter draft, not a signed contract.
Paste the notes as-is rather than pre-writing a narrative from them.
Ask for a fixed structure: project understanding, proposed scope of services, fee structure placeholder, timeline placeholder, and standard terms placeholder.
Instruct the model not to invent a fee amount, phase breakdown, or scope item beyond what your notes or firm standards specify.
Review the draft against your notes and add your actual fee, phase breakdown, and contract terms yourself.
Route the completed letter through your firm's standard proposal review before sending to the client.
lessons.prompt:
You are helping me draft a first-pass project proposal and fee letter from client meeting notes. This is a draft for my review - not a final proposal or contract, and it contains no invented fee amounts or contract terms.

Rules:
- Use ONLY the project understanding stated in the notes below. Do not add scope items, site conditions, or client goals not mentioned.
- Do not generate a specific fee amount, percentage, or phase breakdown - leave [FEE TO BE DETERMINED BY FIRM] as a placeholder.
- Do not generate contract terms (liability, insurance, termination clauses) - leave [STANDARD FIRM TERMS TO BE INSERTED] as a placeholder.
- Keep the 'Project Understanding' section closely reflecting what's in the notes, not embellished.

Draft a proposal/fee letter with this structure:
1. Project understanding (from notes)
2. Proposed scope of services (based on typical phases for this project type, clearly marked as a starting point for my review)
3. Fee structure - [PLACEHOLDER]
4. Anticipated timeline - [PLACEHOLDER, note any timeline mentioned in notes]
5. Standard terms - [PLACEHOLDER]

Meeting notes:
[PASTE RAW MEETING NOTES]
Project type: [e.g. single-family residential addition, commercial tenant fit-out]
lessons.explanation: Keeping the project-understanding section tightly grounded in your actual notes, rather than letting the model embellish the client's goals, protects you from sending a proposal that subtly misstates what the client actually asked for - a bad first impression before the relationship even starts. The fee, phase-breakdown, and contract-terms placeholders exist because those numbers reflect your firm's actual cost structure, risk tolerance, and standard terms - not something a language model can responsibly estimate. Letting it draft a reasonable scope-of-services starting point for a familiar project type is useful precisely because it's the least risky part to generate and the easiest for you to edit.
lessons.example:
Meeting notes: 'Client wants 800sf addition to single-family home, kitchen expansion + new sunroom, wants to start construction next spring, mentioned budget around $150-200k for construction, has an engineer they've worked with before for structural.' Project type: single-family residential addition.

Output draft: 'Project Understanding: Client is seeking an approximately 800 SF addition to their single-family residence, including a kitchen expansion and new sunroom, with an anticipated construction start in spring [year] and a stated construction budget range of $150,000-$200,000. Client has an existing relationship with a structural engineer for this project. Proposed Scope of Services: Schematic Design, Design Development, Construction Documents, Bidding/Negotiation Assistance, Construction Administration [note: typical phases for this project type - confirm against firm standard]. Fee Structure: [FEE TO BE DETERMINED BY FIRM]. Anticipated Timeline: Construction start noted as spring [year] in meeting - confirm design/permitting timeline accordingly. Standard Terms: [STANDARD FIRM TERMS TO BE INSERTED].' Nothing about budget or client goals was invented or expanded beyond the notes.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, draft a proposal from real or practice meeting notes using this prompt, then fill in your actual fee, phase breakdown, and standard terms before treating it as ready to send.
lessons.expectedResult: A structured proposal/fee letter draft where the project-understanding section accurately reflects only what was discussed, with fee and contract-term placeholders clearly marked for you to complete before the letter goes to the client.
commonMistakes: Sending a draft with the fee or terms placeholder still showing, or letting the model's placeholder scope-of-services stand in for your actual firm standard without review.
Letting the project-understanding section embellish or assume client goals beyond what was actually discussed in the meeting.
Skipping your firm's standard proposal review process because the AI draft looks polished and complete.
Reusing a scope-of-services list across a materially different project type without checking it against that project's actual needs.
lessons.proTip: Keep your firm's standard phase-by-phase scope-of-services language as a reference block you paste into the prompt - it keeps the generated scope section consistent with what your firm actually delivers instead of generic industry phase names.

lessons.title: Write a concept narrative that sells your design with Claude or ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn your design intent and key moves into a compelling concept narrative for a client presentation, planning submission, or competition entry.
lessons.goal: Produce a persuasive, accurate concept narrative built from your actual design decisions, ready to accompany drawings in a presentation or submission.
lessons.whyItMatters: A design can be strong and still fail to land if the story around it is flat or generic - clients, juries, and planning boards respond to a narrative that makes the design's logic clear. AI is useful for turning your design intent into polished, persuasive prose quickly, but the narrative has to describe decisions you actually made for real site, program, and client reasons - never invented design moves the drawings don't actually show.
steps: List your actual design decisions and the reasons behind them: site response, program organization, material choices, key formal moves.
State the audience and purpose: client presentation, planning submission, competition entry, awards entry.
Paste your design decisions as notes, not polished prose - let the AI do the narrative structuring.
Ask for a narrative that ties each design move back to a stated reason (site, program, client goal, or context) rather than abstract design language.
Instruct the model not to describe any material, form, or spatial feature not in your notes.
Read the narrative against your actual drawings and correct any description that doesn't match what's actually designed.
Adjust tone and length for the specific audience before finalizing - a jury narrative and a client-facing narrative read differently.
lessons.prompt:
You are helping me write a concept narrative for [AUDIENCE/PURPOSE: e.g. client presentation, planning submission, competition entry]. This narrative must accurately describe a real design - do not invent design features, materials, or moves that aren't in my notes below.

Design decisions and reasoning (my notes):
[LIST YOUR ACTUAL DESIGN MOVES AND WHY - SITE RESPONSE, PROGRAM ORGANIZATION, MATERIALS, KEY FORMAL MOVES]
Project type/context: [BRIEFLY DESCRIBE]

Rules:
- Every design move described must come from my notes above - do not add materials, forms, or spatial features not mentioned.
- Tie each move back to a stated reason (site condition, program need, client goal, or context) rather than using generic design language ('elegant,' 'timeless') without grounding it in a specific decision.
- Match the tone to the audience: [state desired tone, e.g. 'persuasive but professional for a client' or 'precise and technical for a planning board'].

Write a concept narrative of approximately [LENGTH, e.g. 300-400 words].
lessons.explanation: Anchoring the narrative strictly to your own listed design decisions prevents the most common failure mode in AI-assisted design writing: fluent, confident prose describing a feature that doesn't actually exist in the drawings, which is embarrassing at best and misleading in a formal submission at worst. Requiring every move to tie back to a stated reason - rather than floating adjectives - is what makes a concept narrative persuasive in the first place; juries and clients respond to design logic, not vocabulary. Matching tone to audience matters because the same design deserves a different narrative voice in a client deck versus a planning board submission versus a competition entry.
lessons.example:
Design notes: 'Site slopes 8ft east to west, house is split-level to follow grade instead of requiring retaining walls, main living space oriented south for solar gain and views of existing oak trees the client wanted preserved, exterior material is standing-seam metal to reference the client's request for low maintenance and the agricultural buildings nearby.' Audience: client presentation, persuasive but professional tone.

Output narrative: 'The design begins with the site itself: an eight-foot grade change from east to west that we chose to work with rather than against. Instead of cutting into the slope and building retaining walls, the house steps down in a split-level section that follows the existing grade - reducing site disturbance and preserving the mature oak trees you asked us to protect. The main living spaces face south, opening toward the oaks and drawing in daylight through the day. On the exterior, standing-seam metal siding answers two goals at once: the low-maintenance material you asked for, and a quiet nod to the agricultural buildings nearby that gave this site its character long before we arrived.' Every material, orientation, and formal move traces directly to a note; nothing was invented.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, list the real design decisions for a current project and generate a narrative for a specific audience using this prompt. Check the narrative against your actual drawings before using it.
lessons.expectedResult: A polished concept narrative where every described design move, material, and spatial decision matches what's actually shown in your drawings, appropriately toned for the stated audience.
commonMistakes: Letting the model add a plausible-sounding material or formal move that isn't actually part of the design, which becomes an embarrassing mismatch when drawings are shown alongside it.
Using generic design adjectives without tying them to an actual stated reason, which reads as filler to an experienced client or jury.
Reusing the same narrative tone for a planning board submission and a client pitch, when the two audiences need different framing.
Skipping the check against your actual drawings because the narrative sounds convincing on its own.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running notes file per project logging why each major design decision was made as you make it - when it's time to write the narrative, you'll have real, specific reasoning to draw from instead of reconstructing your own logic from memory under deadline.

lessons.title: Explore visual design concepts with GPT Image 2 and Nano Banana
lessons.summary: Use ChatGPT's GPT Image 2 or Gemini's Nano Banana to quickly explore massing, material, and mood directions for early concept work - clearly labeled as illustrative exploration, never construction documents.
lessons.goal: Generate a set of AI image concept explorations for massing, material, or mood direction that speed up early design conversations, always labeled as non-dimensional illustrative studies.
lessons.whyItMatters: Early concept exploration benefits from seeing many directions fast, and today's AI image tools can generate massing studies, material moods, and atmosphere images in minutes instead of hours of manual sketching or rendering. ChatGPT's GPT Image 2 is a strong instruction-follower and handles composition and in-image text well; Gemini's Nano Banana is particularly strong for mood boards, material palettes, and conversational, iterative editing ('make the roof steeper,' 'warmer material tones'). This is genuinely useful for client conversations and internal design discussion at the earliest stage - but these images are not to scale, not dimensionally accurate, and not a substitute for the architect's own design development, drawings, or construction documents. Every image needs a clear label saying so before it leaves your desk.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A clear sense of what you're exploring - massing, material palette, or mood/atmosphere - and enough project context (site, program, client direction) to generate useful, relevant images rather than generic ones. A ChatGPT account (GPT Image 2 generates images directly in chat) or a Gemini account (Nano Banana is Google's native image model in the Gemini app) - either works; Gemini suits fast, conversational, iterative rounds, ChatGPT suits precise instruction-following or accurate text/labels in the image.
steps: Choose your tool for this round: ChatGPT (GPT Image 2) for precise instruction-following or accurate text/labels in the image, or Gemini (Nano Banana) for fast, conversational, iterative editing of a mood or material direction.
Decide what you're exploring: massing/form options, a material and color palette, or overall mood/atmosphere - pick one focus per exploration round.
Write a specific prompt describing the project context: building type, site character, scale, and the design direction or constraint you're testing.
Generate multiple variations rather than accepting the first result - concept exploration works best as a spread of options to react to.
Review each image critically against real project constraints (site, program, budget) that the image generator has no knowledge of.
Select the directions worth developing further and note specifically what you're taking from each image - a massing idea, a material feel, a proportion.
Label every image used in a presentation or client conversation as an illustrative concept study, not a rendering, drawing, or accurate representation of the final design.
Develop the selected direction through your own drawings and design process - the AI image is a starting spark, not a design deliverable.
lessons.prompt:
Generate [NUMBER, e.g. 4-6] concept exploration images for early-stage architectural design, focused on [FOCUS: massing/form, material palette, or mood/atmosphere].

Project context: [BUILDING TYPE, SCALE, SITE CHARACTER, CLIMATE/REGION]
Design direction or constraint being explored: [e.g. 'how a pitched-roof form could relate to the sloped site and existing tree line', or 'a warm, textured material palette responding to a client who wants natural materials with low maintenance']
Style/reference notes: [ANY REFERENCE BUILDINGS, MATERIALS, OR PRECEDENTS TO DRAW FROM]

Generate a range of distinct directions rather than close variations of one idea.
lessons.explanation: Fixing one focus per round - massing, material, or mood, not all three at once - keeps each batch of images useful for a specific design conversation instead of a muddled mix that's hard to react to productively. Asking for a range of distinct directions rather than near-duplicates is what makes this a genuine exploration tool rather than a single-image gamble. GPT Image 2 tends to follow detailed compositional instructions and render text or labels more reliably, while Nano Banana is built for fast conversational editing - both are good fits for this kind of iterative round. The labeling discipline in the last two steps is the real safeguard in this lesson: these images have no dimensional accuracy, no structural logic, and no relationship to actual buildable geometry, and presenting one without that context - to a client, a jury, or your own team - risks setting an expectation the real design and drawings may not be able to meet.
lessons.example:
Focus: massing/form. Project context: a two-story single-family home on a wooded, gently sloped lot in a temperate climate. Design direction: exploring how a simple gabled form could break into two offset volumes to preserve views through the site and reduce apparent bulk from the street.

Output: a set of 5 distinct massing studies showing different ways two offset gabled volumes could relate - varying roof pitch, offset distance, and connector form - used in an internal design meeting to react to which offset relationship felt most successful, before the architect develops the selected direction into an actual scaled massing model and site-responsive drawings. Each image presented in the client meeting is labeled 'Illustrative concept study - not a rendering or final design' in the presentation.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT or Gemini account, generate a set of massing or material concept images for a real or practice project, using a specific focus and real project context. Select one direction and sketch or model it yourself to test whether it actually works dimensionally on the real site.
lessons.expectedResult: A set of distinct, project-relevant concept images that sparked or clarified a real design direction, clearly labeled as illustrative studies wherever shown, with the selected direction carried forward into your own scaled design development - not used as a stand-in for drawings.
commonMistakes: Presenting an AI-generated concept image to a client without a clear 'illustrative concept study, not a final design or rendering' label, which can set an inaccurate expectation.
Treating a visually appealing generated image as dimensionally or structurally feasible without checking it against the real site and program constraints.
Mixing massing, material, and mood exploration into one vague prompt, which produces images too unfocused to usefully react to.
Skipping your own design development and treating the selected image itself as the design, rather than as a starting spark you develop through actual drawings.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running visual library per project of the concept images that led somewhere - even the ones you didn't pursue - and note briefly why. Reviewing it later in the project often surfaces a discarded direction that solves a problem that came up afterward.

lessons.title: Draft client-facing project documentation and status updates with Claude or ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn internal project notes into clear, professional client-facing updates and documentation - covering progress, decisions needed, and next steps.
lessons.goal: Produce accurate, well-organized client-facing project updates built strictly from facts and decisions you supply, ready for your review before sending.
lessons.whyItMatters: Clients judge a project's health as much by how well they're kept informed as by the design itself, and writing a clear, well-organized update for every milestone or delay is time consuming to do well and often gets skipped under deadline pressure. AI can turn your internal project notes into a clean, client-ready update quickly - but only you know what's actually confirmed, what's still pending, and what tone is appropriate for a specific client relationship, especially when the update involves a delay, cost change, or decision the client needs to make.
steps: Gather your internal project notes: what's been completed, what's pending, any decisions the client needs to make, and any delays or changes.
State the update's purpose and the client relationship context (a routine milestone update, a delay notice, a decision request).
Paste your raw notes rather than a pre-written update - let the AI do the structuring and tone work.
Ask for a structure that separates what's done, what's in progress, what decision is needed from the client (if any), and next steps with dates.
Instruct the model not to add any status, cause, or reassurance not stated in your notes - especially around delays or cost.
Review the draft for tone and accuracy, and personally add anything requiring your judgment about how to frame a sensitive update.
Send the update yourself after review - never send an AI draft covering a delay, cost change, or client decision unedited.
lessons.prompt:
You are helping me draft a client-facing project update. This is a draft for my review before sending - it must not overstate certainty or add reassurance not stated in my notes.

Rules:
- Use ONLY the facts in the notes below. Do not add project status, causes for delay, or reassurances I haven't stated.
- Where a sentence would require my own judgment about how to frame a sensitive update (a delay, cost change, or difficult decision), insert a bracketed placeholder like [ARCHITECT TO ADD FRAMING] rather than writing something plausible-sounding.
- Keep tone professional and appropriately warm without overpromising on timeline or outcome.

Draft a client update covering:
Purpose: [e.g. routine milestone update, delay notice, decision request]
What's completed: [LIST FROM NOTES]
What's in progress: [LIST FROM NOTES]
Decision needed from client (if any): [STATE OR WRITE 'NONE']
Next steps and dates: [LIST FROM NOTES]

Structure the update with clear headers for each section above, and label it 'DRAFT - review before sending' at the top.
lessons.explanation: Separating completed, in-progress, decisions-needed, and next-steps into fixed sections is what makes a client update actually actionable rather than a wall of narrative text the client has to parse for what matters. The [ARCHITECT TO ADD FRAMING] placeholder is the key safeguard for anything sensitive - a schedule slip or cost increase needs judgment about tone and framing that reflects your actual relationship with that specific client, which a generic draft cannot supply. The 'DRAFT - review before sending' label is deliberate friction so a fast-turnaround update never goes out unread, especially the ones covering a delay or a decision the client needs to make.
lessons.example:
Notes supplied: 'Permit review taking longer than expected - city comments came back 2 weeks late, we're revising drawings now, resubmitting in 5 business days. Client needs to decide on kitchen appliance package by end of month or it delays the order. Site survey completed, no issues found.' Purpose: delay notice + decision request.

Output draft: 'DRAFT - review before sending. Subject: Project Update - [Project Name]. Completed: Site survey is complete with no issues identified. In Progress: We received city comments on the permit submission and are revising the drawings now; resubmission is planned within 5 business days. [ARCHITECT TO ADD FRAMING: note on what this means for overall schedule]. Decision Needed: To keep the appliance order on schedule, we'll need your kitchen appliance package selection by [date, end of month]. Next Steps: Resubmit permit drawings by [date]; awaiting your appliance decision by [date].' The architect then fills in the bracketed schedule framing with their own judgment about how much reassurance is appropriate before sending.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, draft a client update from real or practice project notes using this prompt, then personally write the framing for any sensitive section before treating it as ready to send.
lessons.expectedResult: A clearly structured client update that accurately reflects only the facts you supplied, with any sensitive framing left as a placeholder for your own judgment, reviewed and edited by you before sending.
commonMistakes: Sending an AI-drafted delay or cost-change notice without personally reviewing and adding your own framing first.
Letting the model supply a reassurance ('this won't affect the schedule') that you haven't actually confirmed is true.
Burying a decision the client needs to make inside narrative prose instead of the fixed 'decision needed' section where it can't be missed.
Reusing an update template across very different client relationships without adjusting tone for how that specific client prefers to be communicated with.
lessons.proTip: Keep a short profile per client noting their communication preferences (e.g. 'wants headline first, details after' or 'prefers phone call for anything involving cost') and paste it into the prompt as a style note - it keeps updates consistent with how each client actually wants to hear from you.

lessons.title: Draft planning and consent application documents with compliance guardrails
lessons.summary: Produce a first draft of a planning or consent application narrative and supporting document grounded in your actual project facts, with everything code- or zoning-sensitive clearly flagged for verification.
lessons.goal: Produce a grounded first draft of a planning/consent submission narrative or design statement, with every zoning, code, or ordinance-sensitive claim flagged for independent verification against the current adopted regulations.
lessons.whyItMatters: Planning and consent submissions - design statements, variance narratives, heritage or conservation area statements - need to be persuasive and precise at the same time, and a document that misstates a zoning figure or ordinance reference can delay or derail an approval. AI can draft a strong, well-organized narrative from your actual project facts, but zoning codes, overlay districts, and ordinance requirements vary by jurisdiction and change over time - every regulatory claim in the draft has to be verified against the current, official source before submission, never taken on the model's word.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Your actual project facts (site data, zoning district, proposed use, dimensional data) and, ideally, the current zoning ordinance or planning code text for the relevant jurisdiction to check citations against.
steps: Gather the actual project facts: site address, zoning district, proposed use, key dimensional data (setbacks, height, FAR, lot coverage) as you've calculated them.
State the submission type: variance narrative, design statement, conservation area statement, site plan narrative, etc., and the jurisdiction.
Paste your project facts and any specific zoning/ordinance sections you already know apply - don't ask the model to identify the applicable code from scratch.
Ask for a narrative structured around the standard sections your jurisdiction requires (project description, compliance summary, any variance justification).
Instruct the model to flag every zoning figure, ordinance section, or compliance claim with [VERIFY AGAINST CURRENT ORDINANCE] rather than asserting compliance or citing a section number itself.
Independently verify every flagged item against the current official zoning ordinance or planning code text before anything is submitted.
Route the completed draft through your firm's standard review and, where required, have it reviewed by planning counsel before submission.
lessons.prompt:
You are helping me draft a planning/consent submission document from project facts I provide. This is a first draft for my review - not a final submission, and it must not assert code or zoning compliance on its own authority.

Rules:
- Use ONLY the project facts provided below. Do not add site conditions, dimensional data, or zoning figures not stated.
- For every statement involving a zoning figure, ordinance section, setback, height limit, use classification, or compliance claim, add the tag [VERIFY AGAINST CURRENT ORDINANCE] - do not state compliance as settled fact or cite a specific section number as authoritative.
- Do not predict whether an approval will be granted or characterize the strength of the application.
- Keep the tone factual and persuasive where appropriate (e.g. a variance justification), but never overstate certainty about a regulatory point.

Draft a [SUBMISSION TYPE] for:
Jurisdiction: [STATE JURISDICTION]
Project facts: [SITE ADDRESS, ZONING DISTRICT, PROPOSED USE, KEY DIMENSIONAL DATA]
Known applicable zoning/ordinance sections (if any): [LIST OR WRITE 'UNKNOWN - FLAG FOR RESEARCH']

Structure: project description, site and zoning context, compliance summary (with verification flags), and [IF APPLICABLE: variance/exception justification].
lessons.explanation: Feeding the model your own already-calculated dimensional data, rather than asking it to determine setbacks or FAR itself, keeps the highest-risk numbers under your direct control from the start. The [VERIFY AGAINST CURRENT ORDINANCE] tag is the load-bearing safeguard in this lesson: zoning ordinances are hyperlocal, frequently amended, and often layered with overlay districts or variance history the model has no way to know about, so every regulatory assertion has to be treated as a draft claim pending your own check against the actual current code text - never submitted on the strength of the AI's phrasing alone. Banning predictions about approval odds keeps the document focused on describing the project accurately rather than editorializing about outcomes that are the planning board's call, not the model's.
lessons.example:
Project facts: site at a specific address, zoned R-2 residential, proposing a rear addition that would reduce the rear setback from the required 25ft to 18ft due to an irregular lot shape, existing structure is non-conforming on a side setback already. Submission type: variance narrative.

Output draft (excerpt): 'Project Description: The proposed addition adds approximately 400 SF to the rear of the existing single-family residence. Site and Zoning Context: The property is zoned R-2. [VERIFY AGAINST CURRENT ORDINANCE: confirm current R-2 rear setback requirement, stated here as 25 ft per project facts provided.] The irregular, pie-shaped lot geometry results in a rear setback of approximately 18 ft for the proposed addition. Variance Justification: The lot's non-standard shape, rather than any choice to maximize buildable area, is the source of the setback reduction. [VERIFY AGAINST CURRENT ORDINANCE: confirm the specific variance criteria this jurisdiction requires be addressed, e.g. hardship, self-created hardship exclusion, minimum variance necessary.]' The architect then confirms the actual current setback requirement and variance criteria against the official zoning ordinance before finalizing the narrative.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, draft a planning/consent narrative for a real or practice project using this prompt. Independently verify at least two flagged zoning figures or ordinance sections against your jurisdiction's current official code text before treating the draft as accurate.
lessons.expectedResult: A well-structured planning/consent narrative built from your actual project facts, with every zoning figure and ordinance reference clearly flagged, and at least the flagged items you've personally verified against the current official code confirmed accurate before submission.
commonMistakes: Submitting a draft with an unverified zoning figure or ordinance citation the model generated or restated without independent confirmation.
Letting the narrative imply or predict that an approval is likely, which oversteps into a judgment the planning authority alone makes.
Skipping verification of overlay districts, recent ordinance amendments, or site-specific variance history that a general narrative draft has no way to know about.
Treating a draft built for one jurisdiction's submission format as reusable for a different jurisdiction without checking their specific required sections.
lessons.proTip: Before drafting, pull the actual current ordinance sections and dimensional requirements yourself and paste them into the prompt as known facts rather than letting the draft carry placeholder verification flags for basic figures you already have - this narrows what still needs independent research and speeds up your review.

lessons.title: Write portfolio and case-study copy for your practice with Claude or ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn a completed project's facts and outcomes into polished portfolio copy and a case study that accurately represents the work and helps win new clients.
lessons.goal: Produce accurate, persuasive portfolio and case-study copy for a completed project, built strictly from real project facts and outcomes, ready for review before publishing.
lessons.whyItMatters: A strong portfolio is how most architecture practices win new work, and writing genuinely persuasive case-study copy for every completed project is a task that constantly loses out to billable deadlines. AI can turn your project facts into polished marketing copy quickly, but a portfolio piece that overstates your role, invents a design outcome, or misstates a project fact is a credibility risk the moment a prospective client, juror, or former collaborator notices the gap between the copy and reality.
lessons.beforeYouStart: The real project facts: your firm's actual role and scope, key design decisions and why, any measurable outcomes (sustainability metrics, budget/schedule performance, awards), and clearance to publish project images and client name (or agreement to anonymize).
steps: Gather accurate project facts: your firm's actual scope and role, key design decisions and reasoning, any measurable outcomes, and awards or recognition.
Confirm you have the right to publish the project images, client name, and any metrics - anonymize or omit anything you don't have clearance for.
Paste your project facts as notes, not pre-written marketing copy - let the AI do the persuasive structuring.
Ask for a structure that separates project overview, design challenge and response, and outcomes, ending with a specific, factual summary line.
Instruct the model not to add any outcome, metric, award, or design feature not in your notes, and not to overstate your firm's role on a collaborative project.
Review the copy against your actual project record and correct anything that overstates certainty, scope, or outcome.
Have a colleague who worked on the project review the draft for accuracy before it's published.
lessons.prompt:
You are helping me write portfolio and case-study copy for a completed project, for marketing use. This copy must accurately represent the real project - do not invent outcomes, metrics, awards, or overstate my firm's role.

Project facts (my notes):
Firm's actual scope/role: [STATE - e.g. 'design architect, collaborated with XYZ Engineering on structure']
Key design decisions and reasoning: [LIST]
Measurable outcomes (if any): [e.g. energy performance, budget/schedule, awards - or write 'NONE TO CLAIM']
Clearance to publish: [CONFIRM CLIENT NAME/IMAGES ARE CLEARED, OR STATE WHAT MUST BE ANONYMIZED]

Rules:
- Use ONLY the facts provided above. Do not add outcomes, metrics, or awards not stated.
- Do not overstate the firm's role - if the project was collaborative, reflect that accurately rather than implying sole authorship.
- Where I've noted anonymization is needed, do not include the real client name or identifying project details.
- Persuasive tone is appropriate, but every specific claim must be traceable to a fact I provided.

Write: (1) a 40-60 word portfolio summary for a project listing page, and (2) a 300-400 word case study covering project overview, design challenge and response, and outcomes.
lessons.explanation: Requiring the firm's actual scope and role to be stated up front, and instructing the model not to overstate it, matters because portfolio copy is one of the few places a small inaccuracy compounds reputational risk directly - a former collaborator or client who sees their contribution erased or a metric that was never actually measured is a real relationship cost, not just a style problem. Splitting the deliverable into a short listing summary and a longer case study matches how the copy actually gets used across a website or submission, so you get both without a second prompt. Requiring a colleague review before publishing catches inaccuracies the original notes-taker might not remember correctly months or years after project completion.
lessons.example:
Project facts: firm was design architect on a small library renovation, collaborated with a structural engineering firm on seismic retrofit, key decision was preserving original reading room daylighting while adding accessible entry, project came in on budget, won a local AIA chapter award for adaptive reuse. Clearance: client name and images cleared for publication.

Output portfolio summary: 'A careful adaptive reuse of a 1930s branch library, preserving its landmark reading room daylighting while adding full accessibility and a seismic retrofit - completed on budget and recognized with a [Local Chapter] AIA Adaptive Reuse Award.' Case study (excerpt): 'When [Client] approached us to renovate their historic branch library, the challenge was clear: bring the century-old building up to current accessibility and seismic standards without compromising the reading room's original daylighting, long considered the building's defining feature. Working with [Structural Engineering Firm] on the seismic retrofit, we developed a discreet reinforcement strategy that preserved the room's original clerestory windows...' The structural engineer's role is credited accurately, and every claim - the award, the on-budget outcome, the daylighting preservation - traces to a stated fact.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, write portfolio and case-study copy for a real completed project using this prompt. Have a colleague who worked on the project review it for accuracy before you consider it ready to publish.
lessons.expectedResult: Polished, persuasive portfolio and case-study copy where every claimed outcome, metric, and role accurately reflects the real project, reviewed by a colleague who worked on it, with any required anonymization correctly applied before publishing.
commonMistakes: Letting the copy imply sole authorship on a collaborative project, which damages professional relationships when the omission is noticed.
Publishing a metric or award claim that was never actually confirmed or measured, discovered later by a prospective client doing diligence.
Skipping colleague review because the copy reads well, missing a factual error only someone else on the project would catch.
Publishing client-identifying details or images without confirming you actually have clearance to use them.
lessons.proTip: Build a standing project-facts file for every completed project as it wraps up - scope, role, outcomes, clearance status - while the details are fresh, instead of trying to reconstruct them accurately from memory when it's time to write the case study months or years later.
